lessons.title: Professional standards and communication
content: Arrive on time, prepared and fit for duty. Allow enough time to be ready before the vehicle is due to leave.
Follow Swans Travel's dress and presentation standard. Your conduct and appearance represent the company to passengers, clients and the public.
Be polite, calm, helpful and respectful. Do not argue with passengers, colleagues or other road users. If a situation becomes difficult, keep people safe and contact the office.
Never use a handheld phone while driving. Follow company rules for other devices and distractions.
Protect passenger information. Do not share personal details or photographs without permission, including on social media or personal messaging groups.
Safety and legal compliance always come before keeping to a timetable.

slides.heading: You represent Swans Travel
slides.body: A passenger's experience is shaped by the driver they meet. Professional standards are not just about being polite. They include being ready for duty, presenting yourself appropriately, following instructions and making sound decisions throughout the job.
slides.example: Before a school or private hire journey, arrive prepared, check the job information and make sure you understand the collection, destination and any passenger requirements.
slides.takeaway: Be prepared, professional and respectful from the start of every duty.

slides.heading: Communication is part of the job
slides.body: Good communication starts before departure. Confirm the job details, timings, route and any special instructions. During the journey, provide clear and courteous updates and tell the office promptly about delays, route problems or changes. At the end, report completion and anything that needs follow-up.
slides.example: If traffic means you may miss the planned arrival time, tell the office when it is safe to do so. Do not wait until the job has finished.
slides.takeaway: If a detail matters, check it. Do not guess.

slides.heading: Protect passengers and the company's reputation
slides.body: Stay calm if a passenger or road user becomes difficult. Do not argue or allow a disagreement to distract you from driving. Never use a handheld phone while driving. Passenger details and photographs must be kept private and must not be shared without permission.
slides.example: A passenger complains angrily about a delay. Listen, explain what you know accurately and contact the office if the issue needs managing. Do not make promises you cannot authorise.
slides.takeaway: Calm conduct, safe decisions and respect for privacy are expected every time.

slides.heading: Professional judgement when the pressure is on
slides.body: Professional conduct is not just being polite. It is making reliable decisions when the job changes, a passenger is unhappy or the timetable is slipping. You must communicate facts clearly, avoid promises you cannot authorise and never let pressure change a safe decision. A calm, factual handover helps the next person understand what has happened and what still needs doing.
slides.example: A passenger says the coach is late and demands that you use a faster route through a narrow residential street. A professional response is to acknowledge the frustration, explain that you will use a suitable safe route and contact the office if the plan needs changing.
slides.takeaway: Professionalism means calm communication and sound judgement, especially under pressure.

slides.heading: Privacy is part of passenger care
slides.body: Passenger names, contact details, travel arrangements, photographs and information about a person's needs must be treated carefully. Do not share passenger information in group chats or on social media. Only pass information to people who need it for the job, using the company's approved process. If information is sent to the wrong person or a device is lost, report it promptly rather than trying to hide it.
slides.example: You take a photograph of a lost item that also shows a passenger list. Do not post it in a driver group. Use the approved lost-property process and keep personal details out of the image.
slides.takeaway: Only collect, use and share passenger information when it is necessary and authorised.

scenario.question: A passenger is angry about a delay and demands that you take an unsuitable shortcut. What is the best response?
options: Use the shortcut to keep the passenger happy
Stay calm, explain you will use a safe suitable route and contact the office if needed
Tell the passenger to complain when they arrive
Ignore the passenger and say nothing
scenario.explanation: A professional driver communicates calmly and does not compromise safe route choice to recover time.

lessons.title: End-of-job responsibilities
content: Before leaving the vehicle, park in an authorised safe location and secure it as instructed.
Check the entire passenger saloon for passengers, belongings, damage, cleanliness and anything that may need attention.
Handle lost property through the Swans Travel process. Protect personal information and do not keep items or make informal arrangements with passengers.
Complete job, mileage, defect and incident records accurately and promptly. Include customer concerns and any follow-up required.
Return keys, documents and equipment to the correct place and tell the office when the job is complete.

slides.heading: Finishing a job properly
slides.body: The job is not finished simply because the coach has reached its destination. Park in an authorised safe location and secure the vehicle as instructed. Then check the passenger saloon carefully before leaving it.
slides.example: Walk through the saloon and check seats, floor areas and luggage spaces. Make sure no passenger or belongings have been left behind.
slides.takeaway: Secure the vehicle and check the whole saloon before leaving.

slides.heading: Records, lost property and handover
slides.body: Report lost property through the Swans Travel process and protect personal information. Complete job, mileage, defect and incident records accurately and promptly. Tell the office when the job is complete and flag any customer concern or follow-up action.
slides.example: You find a phone after a journey. Do not keep it or arrange an informal handover. Follow the company lost-property process and report it.
slides.takeaway: Accurate records and a clear handover help the next person do their job.

slides.heading: A proper handover closes the safety loop
slides.body: The job is not finished simply because the passengers have got off. Check the vehicle, passenger saloon, luggage areas and any accessible storage spaces. Report damage, defects, lost property and passenger concerns through the correct process. A clear handover identifies the vehicle, time, location, what was found and who was informed. Do not leave the next driver to discover an unresolved safety issue.
slides.example: You notice a loose seat fitting after the final passenger leaves. Record and report it before handing the vehicle over, even if the next duty is not due to start for several hours.
slides.takeaway: Finish the job by checking, recording and handing over anything that needs action.

scenario.question: At the end of a duty you notice a loose seat fitting, but the next coach duty is not for several hours. What should you do?
options: Leave it for the next driver to find
Only report it if a passenger complains
Record and report it through the defect process before handover
Tighten it yourself without authorisation
scenario.explanation: Defects must be reported promptly so the vehicle can be assessed before further use.

quiz.question: Before starting a duty, what should a driver confirm?
options: Only the destination
The job details, timings, route and passenger requirements
Only the vehicle registration
Nothing if the route is familiar
quiz.explanation: Confirm the full job information and any special instructions before departure.

quiz.question: A passenger becomes argumentative. What is the professional response?
options: Argue back
Ignore any safety concern
Stay calm, avoid arguing, keep people safe and contact the office if needed
Ask another passenger to deal with it
quiz.explanation: Remain calm and professional. If the situation becomes difficult, prioritise safety and contact the office.

quiz.question: When should a driver report a significant delay or route problem?
options: At the end of the shift only
Promptly during the journey when safe to do so
Only if a passenger complains
Only after reaching the depot
quiz.explanation: The office needs timely information to manage the service and communicate changes.

quiz.question: Which statement about handheld phones is correct?
options: Use it briefly at traffic lights
Use it if the road is quiet
Do not use a handheld phone while driving
Use it for navigation while moving
quiz.explanation: The training material states that drivers must not use a handheld phone while driving.

quiz.question: How should passenger information and photographs be handled?
options: Share useful photos in personal group chats
Post passenger details online if names are hidden
Keep them private and do not share without permission
Send them to friends for advice
quiz.explanation: Passenger information and photographs must be protected.

quiz.question: What should be checked before the journey if a passenger has specific requirements?
options: Assume the previous driver handled it
Wait until the passenger complains
Confirm the requirements and any special instructions
Ask other passengers to decide
quiz.explanation: Check passenger needs and special instructions before departure.

quiz.question: What should happen at the end of a job?
options: Leave without telling anyone
Report completion, incidents, lost property, defects and customer concerns
Only report if the vehicle is damaged
Keep lost property until next shift
quiz.explanation: The office should receive completion information and any follow-up issues.

quiz.question: Where should a coach be parked at the end of a job?
options: Anywhere convenient
In a passenger loading area
In an authorised, safe location, secured as instructed
On the roadside with keys inside
quiz.explanation: Park safely in an authorised place and secure the vehicle.

lessons.title: How to carry out a proper coach walkaround
content: Freeway records the walkaround, but tapping through the checklist is not the inspection. You must physically look at the vehicle and assess the condition of the items listed. Complete the check before the vehicle is used on the public highway, preferably immediately before departure. Work methodically, use a torch where needed, and do not rush because a duty is waiting. A previous driver's check does not remove your responsibility to make sure the vehicle is safe when you take charge of it.

From the driving position, check the windscreen and front side windows for damage, dirt or anything obstructing your view. Check mirrors and camera equipment are present, secure, clean and correctly adjusted. Check wipers and washers, horn, seat belt, dashboard instruments and warning lamps. Make sure the cab and footwell are clear and controls can be reached safely. Follow the vehicle-specific procedure for any checks involving the braking or air system.

Inspect every tyre, including inner tyres on twin-wheel arrangements where visible. Look for cuts, bulges, exposed cords, embedded objects, cracking, uneven wear and signs of under-inflation. Look at wheel rims for damage and check that wheel fixings appear present and secure. Check wheel nut indicators where fitted and look for signs that a wheel nut may have moved. Look for objects trapped between twin wheels. Never put yourself under the vehicle or in an unsafe position to inspect something.

Check that headlamps, dipped beam, main beam, side lights, indicators, hazard warning lights, brake lights, rear lights, reflectors and number plates are present, clean, secure and working as required. Use a colleague or an appropriate safe method to confirm brake lights. Look for cracked or missing lenses and lights showing the wrong colour. Check that plates can be read and are not obscured.

Walk around the front, both sides and rear. Look at body panels, bumpers, mirrors, windows, doors, access panels, luggage lockers, fuel and AdBlue areas, mudguards and underbody areas that are safely visible. Look for loose or hanging parts, sharp edges, fresh impact damage, missing fittings and signs of leaks. Check for fuel, oil, coolant or other fluid on the ground or around the vehicle. Do not crawl underneath or attempt a repair.

Check passenger doors open, close and secure correctly. Check emergency exits, their markings and any warning indicators. Make sure aisles and exits are unobstructed. Check seats are secure, seat backs and fittings are not damaged, and seat belts are present and work correctly. Look at steps, handrails, grab rails, parcel racks and interior panels for looseness or damage. Check there are no trip hazards, loose items or anything that could injure a passenger during the journey.

Check the safety equipment required for the vehicle is present, accessible and appears serviceable. Check any fitted wheelchair lift or ramp, wheelchair restraints, accessible equipment, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, emergency hammer, warning equipment and other items in accordance with the vehicle checklist and company procedure. Check height information and any vehicle-specific controls or isolation equipment you are trained to inspect. Do not operate equipment you have not been trained to use.

Complete each item in Freeway based on what you have actually inspected. Record nil defects only when you have completed the check and found no defects. If you find something, select the correct defect, describe the location and symptoms clearly, and add photographs where the app allows and it is safe to do so. Submit the report and make sure it has been recorded. Never select nil defects to get the vehicle released or because you are running late.

slides.heading: A walkaround is a physical inspection
slides.body: Freeway records the walkaround, but tapping through the checklist is not the inspection. You must physically look at the vehicle and assess the condition of the items listed. Complete the check before the vehicle is used on the public highway, preferably immediately before departure. Work methodically, use a torch where needed, and do not rush because a duty is waiting. A previous driver's check does not remove your responsibility to make sure the vehicle is safe when you take charge of it.
slides.example: You have a coach allocated and the departure time is close. You must still complete the inspection properly. If there is not enough time, tell the office rather than submitting a check you have not done.
slides.takeaway: Freeway is the record of the check. Your eyes and your judgement carry out the check.

slides.heading: Start with the cab and visibility
slides.body: From the driving position, check the windscreen and front side windows for damage, dirt or anything obstructing your view. Check mirrors and camera equipment are present, secure, clean and correctly adjusted. Check wipers and washers, horn, seat belt, dashboard instruments and warning lamps. Make sure the cab and footwell are clear and controls can be reached safely. Follow the vehicle-specific procedure for any checks involving the braking or air system.
slides.example: A mirror is loose, a camera screen is not working or the windscreen damage affects your view. Do not assume you can manage without it. Record the issue in Freeway and follow the defect process.
slides.takeaway: You need clear visibility and safe control of the vehicle before moving.

slides.heading: Check tyres and wheels, all of them
slides.body: Inspect every tyre, including inner tyres on twin-wheel arrangements where visible. Look for cuts, bulges, exposed cords, embedded objects, cracking, uneven wear and signs of under-inflation. Look at wheel rims for damage and check that wheel fixings appear present and secure. Check wheel nut indicators where fitted and look for signs that a wheel nut may have moved. Look for objects trapped between twin wheels. Never put yourself under the vehicle or in an unsafe position to inspect something.
slides.example: You see a bulge in a tyre sidewall, exposed cord, a deep cut or a tyre that appears significantly under-inflated. Do not decide it will last one more journey. Record it in Freeway and do not take the vehicle out until Engineering has assessed and cleared it.
slides.takeaway: Tyres and wheels are safety-critical. Check every wheel position, not just the front tyres.

slides.heading: Check lights, indicators and reflectors
slides.body: Check that headlamps, dipped beam, main beam, side lights, indicators, hazard warning lights, brake lights, rear lights, reflectors and number plates are present, clean, secure and working as required. Use a colleague or an appropriate safe method to confirm brake lights. Look for cracked or missing lenses and lights showing the wrong colour. Check that plates can be read and are not obscured.
slides.example: A rear brake light is not working or an indicator lens is broken. Identify exactly which light and its position, report it in Freeway and follow the criticality and clearance process. Do not simply assume it is acceptable because the vehicle still moves.
slides.takeaway: Lights help you see, be seen and communicate with other road users.

slides.heading: Walk the full outside of the coach
slides.body: Walk around the front, both sides and rear. Look at body panels, bumpers, mirrors, windows, doors, access panels, luggage lockers, fuel and AdBlue areas, mudguards and underbody areas that are safely visible. Look for loose or hanging parts, sharp edges, fresh impact damage, missing fittings and signs of leaks. Check for fuel, oil, coolant or other fluid on the ground or around the vehicle. Do not crawl underneath or attempt a repair.
slides.example: A luggage locker does not latch, a panel is hanging loose or there is a fresh fluid leak. These are not cosmetic details to ignore. Record what you can see in Freeway and seek the correct assessment before the vehicle is used.
slides.takeaway: Look high and low, front to rear, on both sides.

slides.heading: Check doors, exits and the passenger saloon
slides.body: Check passenger doors open, close and secure correctly. Check emergency exits, their markings and any warning indicators. Make sure aisles and exits are unobstructed. Check seats are secure, seat backs and fittings are not damaged, and seat belts are present and work correctly. Look at steps, handrails, grab rails, parcel racks and interior panels for looseness or damage. Check there are no trip hazards, loose items or anything that could injure a passenger during the journey.
slides.example: A seat is loose, a belt will not latch or luggage is blocking an emergency exit. Do not carry passengers and hope nobody notices. Report the exact location and issue in Freeway and wait for the appropriate decision.
slides.takeaway: A safe passenger saloon means secure seats, working restraints and clear exits.

slides.heading: Check safety equipment and vehicle-specific items
slides.body: Check the safety equipment required for the vehicle is present, accessible and appears serviceable. Check any fitted wheelchair lift or ramp, wheelchair restraints, accessible equipment, fire extinguisher, first aid kit, emergency hammer, warning equipment and other items in accordance with the vehicle checklist and company procedure. Check height information and any vehicle-specific controls or isolation equipment you are trained to inspect. Do not operate equipment you have not been trained to use.
slides.example: A wheelchair restraint is missing or a lift shows a fault. Do not improvise or tell a passenger it will be fine. Record it in Freeway and contact Engineering or the office for direction.
slides.takeaway: Check the equipment fitted to that particular coach, not just what you remember from another vehicle.

slides.heading: Finish the check honestly in Freeway
slides.body: Complete each item in Freeway based on what you have actually inspected. Record nil defects only when you have completed the check and found no defects. If you find something, select the correct defect, describe the location and symptoms clearly, and add photographs where the app allows and it is safe to do so. Submit the report and make sure it has been recorded. Never select nil defects to get the vehicle released or because you are running late.
slides.example: A tyre has a visible cut. Do not submit a nil-defect check and mention the tyre verbally later. Record the actual defect in Freeway so there is a traceable record for Engineering and the operator.
slides.takeaway: The Freeway record must match the real condition of the coach.

slides.heading: Look for evidence, not just a tick-box
slides.body: A walkaround is an inspection, not a memory test. Look at the component, check its condition and ask whether it could affect safe operation. Compare the left and right sides where useful. Look for changes such as fresh damage, missing fixings, fluid marks, tyre bulges, exposed cords, insecure panels or signs of rubbing. If a check cannot be completed properly, do not record it as satisfactory.
slides.example: A tyre may look inflated from a distance but have a sidewall bulge. Walk close enough to inspect the whole visible tyre and do not rely on appearance from the cab.
slides.takeaway: A completed checklist is only useful when the physical inspection has actually been done.

slides.heading: Know what a defect report must achieve
slides.body: A useful report allows Engineering to identify the vehicle, understand the symptom, assess its significance and decide what inspection or repair is needed. State what you observed, where it is, when it happened and whether it changed. Avoid vague entries such as 'noise' or 'something wrong'. Do not diagnose beyond your knowledge and never downgrade a concern just to keep the vehicle moving.
slides.example: Instead of writing 'brakes noisy', describe when the noise occurs, whether there is vibration or a warning, which end of the vehicle it appears to come from and whether it began during the journey.
slides.takeaway: Describe observable facts precisely, then let the authorised engineering process assess the defect.

scenario.question: You see a tyre with a visible sidewall bulge, but it is holding air. What is the right decision?
options: Use it for a short local journey
Record it as a minor observation and continue
Do not use the vehicle, report the defect and await assessment
Ask another driver if they think it looks acceptable
scenario.explanation: A sidewall bulge can indicate structural tyre damage. Do not make an informal decision to use the vehicle.

lessons.title: Using Freeway and reporting defects correctly
content: Freeway is where you complete and submit the vehicle walkaround check and report defects. It also displays vehicle defect status and warnings. Use the app as part of the process, not as a substitute for physically inspecting the coach. Check that you have selected the correct vehicle before starting. Follow the checklist in order and make sure the result is submitted successfully.

Describe what is wrong, where it is, when it happens and any symptoms you noticed. Avoid vague descriptions such as 'faulty', 'not right' or 'noise'. Include the vehicle identification, date and your details as required by Freeway. Add a photograph if the app supports it and it is safe and useful. Do not guess at the technical cause. Report what you observed.

If Freeway shows a critical defect or indicates that the vehicle is not roadworthy, the vehicle must not be driven on the road. Do not acknowledge the warning and carry on. Do not assume the warning is old, a glitch or somebody else's problem. Do not decide for yourself that the defect is safe. Keep the vehicle out of service, tell the office and contact Peter in Engineering for direction. The vehicle can only return to service when the defect has been properly assessed, rectified where necessary and formally cleared through the company process.

Submitting a defect report does not mean the vehicle is repaired or safe. A driver cannot clear a critical defect by pressing a button, adding a comment or deciding that the symptom has disappeared. Do not use a vehicle until the responsible Engineering process has confirmed it is fit for service and the Freeway status and company release process allow it. If the app status and a verbal instruction appear to conflict, stop and get clarification before moving the vehicle.

For an engineering defect or a critical Freeway warning, contact Peter in Engineering and notify the office or duty manager. Give the vehicle registration, the exact Freeway warning or defect, when it appeared, any symptoms and whether passengers are on board. If the defect occurs during a journey, stop in a safe place, protect passengers and contact the office and Engineering. Follow instructions, but never continue if the vehicle remains unsafe or uncleared.

Your responsibility does not end when the walkaround is submitted. Pay attention to warning lights, changes in handling, vibration, noises, smells, leaks, tyre problems and passenger door or equipment faults while driving. If you become aware of a potential safety defect, find a safe place to stop, assess and report it. Record defects found during the journey or on return in Freeway so the next driver and Engineering are not left unaware.

slides.heading: Freeway is the walkaround and defect-reporting system
slides.body: Freeway is where you complete and submit the vehicle walkaround check and report defects. It also displays vehicle defect status and warnings. Use the app as part of the process, not as a substitute for physically inspecting the coach. Check that you have selected the correct vehicle before starting. Follow the checklist in order and make sure the result is submitted successfully.
slides.example: You are allocated vehicle registration A, but the app still shows vehicle B from your previous duty. Stop and select the correct vehicle before completing the check. A correct inspection attached to the wrong vehicle is not a reliable record.
slides.takeaway: Select the right vehicle, inspect it physically, record accurately and submit.

slides.heading: How to write a useful defect report
slides.body: Describe what is wrong, where it is, when it happens and any symptoms you noticed. Avoid vague descriptions such as 'faulty', 'not right' or 'noise'. Include the vehicle identification, date and your details as required by Freeway. Add a photograph if the app supports it and it is safe and useful. Do not guess at the technical cause. Report what you observed.
slides.example: Weak report: 'noise from back'. Better report: 'Loud metallic knocking from nearside rear, heard over bumps, first noticed during walkaround'. Engineering can investigate a clear description much more effectively.
slides.takeaway: Report what you saw, heard or felt, not a diagnosis you cannot confirm.

slides.heading: A critical defect warning means do not take the vehicle out
slides.body: If Freeway shows a critical defect or indicates that the vehicle is not roadworthy, the vehicle must not be driven on the road. Do not acknowledge the warning and carry on. Do not assume the warning is old, a glitch or somebody else's problem. Do not decide for yourself that the defect is safe. Keep the vehicle out of service, tell the office and contact Peter in Engineering for direction. The vehicle can only return to service when the defect has been properly assessed, rectified where necessary and formally cleared through the company process.
slides.example: Freeway displays a critical defect warning, but the duty is due to leave and passengers are waiting. You must not take that coach. Contact the office, explain that Freeway has flagged a critical defect, and contact Peter in Engineering. The office must arrange a suitable alternative vehicle or manage the service.
slides.takeaway: A critical warning is a stop instruction. No journey, no passenger movement, no 'just this once'.

slides.heading: Do not confuse reporting with clearance
slides.body: Submitting a defect report does not mean the vehicle is repaired or safe. A driver cannot clear a critical defect by pressing a button, adding a comment or deciding that the symptom has disappeared. Do not use a vehicle until the responsible Engineering process has confirmed it is fit for service and the Freeway status and company release process allow it. If the app status and a verbal instruction appear to conflict, stop and get clarification before moving the vehicle.
slides.example: You reported a brake warning and the warning light later goes out. That does not prove the cause has been resolved. Keep the vehicle out of service and get Engineering confirmation.
slides.takeaway: Reported is not repaired. A warning disappearing is not the same as formal clearance.

slides.heading: Who to contact and what to say
slides.body: For an engineering defect or a critical Freeway warning, contact Peter in Engineering and notify the office or duty manager. Give the vehicle registration, the exact Freeway warning or defect, when it appeared, any symptoms and whether passengers are on board. If the defect occurs during a journey, stop in a safe place, protect passengers and contact the office and Engineering. Follow instructions, but never continue if the vehicle remains unsafe or uncleared.
slides.example: Say: 'Vehicle YTxx XXX, Freeway is showing a critical defect for the braking system. The warning appeared before departure. The vehicle is parked and I have not taken it out. Please confirm the next steps.'
slides.takeaway: Be clear, factual and prompt. Escalate critical defects immediately.

slides.heading: Defects found during a journey or at the end of duty
slides.body: Your responsibility does not end when the walkaround is submitted. Pay attention to warning lights, changes in handling, vibration, noises, smells, leaks, tyre problems and passenger door or equipment faults while driving. If you become aware of a potential safety defect, find a safe place to stop, assess and report it. Record defects found during the journey or on return in Freeway so the next driver and Engineering are not left unaware.
slides.example: You hear a new grinding noise from a wheel while carrying passengers. Do not wait until you return to the depot if the vehicle may be unsafe. Stop safely, contact the office and follow the defect process.
slides.takeaway: Keep monitoring the vehicle. Report new symptoms immediately, not just at the next walkaround.

slides.heading: A report is not permission to drive
slides.body: Freeway is Swans Travel's walkaround and defect-reporting app. Submitting a defect records the concern, it does not prove the vehicle is safe and it does not authorise a driver to continue. A critical defect warning means the vehicle must remain out of service. Do not acknowledge the warning and carry on, move passengers or use the vehicle 'just this once'. The vehicle needs an Engineering assessment and formal clearance through the company's process.
slides.example: You submit a report for a steering warning and Freeway displays a critical defect. Even if the office is busy and the coach is booked, you do not take it out. Contact the office and Peter in Engineering and wait for formal clearance.
slides.takeaway: Freeway records the defect. Engineering clearance, not the act of reporting, determines whether the vehicle can return to service.

slides.heading: Escalate clearly and preserve the evidence
slides.body: When a critical warning appears, contact the office and Peter in Engineering. Give the vehicle identity, exact warning or symptom, time, location, whether passengers are on board and what action has already been taken. Do not clear, reset or dismiss a warning to make the vehicle appear available. If the defect develops while moving, stop at a safe place, protect passengers and follow instructions. Record the event accurately in Freeway.
slides.example: A warning appears after leaving the depot. Pull in safely, secure the coach, explain the warning and location to the office and Engineering, and do not resume until the vehicle is formally cleared.
slides.takeaway: Stop safely, report accurately and wait for the authorised decision.

scenario.question: Freeway displays a critical defect warning, but the coach is booked and the office is busy. What must happen?
options: Acknowledge the warning and complete the first journey
Ask the passengers whether they are happy to travel
Keep the vehicle out of service, contact the office and Peter in Engineering, and wait for formal clearance
Move the coach to another depot before reporting it
scenario.explanation: A critical warning means no use. Reporting it is not clearance, formal Engineering assessment and clearance are required.

lessons.title: Your legal responsibility for roadworthiness
content: DVSA guidance says drivers are responsible for making sure the vehicle is safe to drive before setting off. A driver must carry out a walkaround check before the journey and report defects in writing to the person responsible for dealing with them. The operator also has duties to maintain vehicles, provide clear written instructions and have a system to remove non-roadworthy vehicles from service. These responsibilities work together. You cannot transfer your responsibility to the app, the depot or another driver.

DVSA guidance expects a walkaround check before use, with at least one check in each 24-hour period that a vehicle is in service. The check should cover the whole vehicle and visible items that can be safely assessed without dismantling. The record should identify the vehicle, date, defects or symptoms, the person reporting and who was told. Nil-defect reporting is also important, but only when the check has genuinely been completed.

If a defect makes the vehicle dangerous or unroadworthy, it must be rectified before the vehicle is used on the road. A driver must not take a vehicle out because the journey is short, the depot is nearby, the timetable is tight or passengers are waiting. Using a public service vehicle in a dangerous condition can lead to serious consequences, including an unlimited fine and imprisonment. The exact legal outcome depends on the facts and offence.

Police and DVSA can stop buses and coaches, inspect roadworthiness and prohibit a vehicle from being driven until problems are fixed. Drivers can be fined and may face prosecution for roadworthiness offences where they are responsible. The Traffic Commissioner can also take action against drivers who fail to carry out adequate walkaround checks, potentially affecting their vocational entitlement. A poor or false record can make the situation worse because it suggests the check was not properly completed.

Before moving, ask yourself: have I checked the correct vehicle, completed the physical walkaround, recorded the result in Freeway, understood any warnings and confirmed that any reported defect has been cleared? If Freeway shows a critical defect or the vehicle is otherwise unsafe, do not drive it. Contact the office and Peter in Engineering. Do not let pressure, convenience or another person's instruction make you take an unsafe vehicle onto the road.

slides.heading: The law places responsibility on the driver too
slides.body: DVSA guidance says drivers are responsible for making sure the vehicle is safe to drive before setting off. A driver must carry out a walkaround check before the journey and report defects in writing to the person responsible for dealing with them. The operator also has duties to maintain vehicles, provide clear written instructions and have a system to remove non-roadworthy vehicles from service. These responsibilities work together. You cannot transfer your responsibility to the app, the depot or another driver.
slides.example: If someone says 'Engineering knows about it' but Freeway still shows a critical defect and there is no clearance, you must not take the vehicle. Knowing about a defect is not the same as making the vehicle roadworthy.
slides.takeaway: The driver and operator both have responsibilities. Never drive a vehicle you know is unsafe.

slides.heading: A check must be meaningful and recorded
